Core toolkit

Six key ideas for analysing Kiss of the Vampire

1

Signs, denotation and connotation Barthes

Definition

A sign combines a signifier (the form we see or hear) with a signified (the idea it brings to mind). Denotation is the literal meaning; connotation is the associated meaning, which depends on culture and context. For Barthes, myth is a connotation so familiar that it seems natural.

In Kiss of the Vampire
  • Blood, bats and vampires: these signs denote their literal objects but connote the monster movie genre.
  • The grey and black palette: connotes a gloomy, eerie location and tone, conventional for the genre.
  • The colour red: connotes danger (the attacking bats, the blood) but also romance, which is echoed by the word “Kiss” in the title.
  • Myth: men as strong protectors or predators and women as prey is presented as a natural order, not a constructed one.
Exam moveTravel the same road each time: what I see → what it suggests → the wider idea it supports.
2

Barthes’ narrative codes Barthes

Definition

Hermeneutic (enigma): mysteries that hold attention. Proairetic (action): signs that create tension and expectation. Semantic: connotations attached to signifiers. Symbolic: larger themes, often built on oppositions. Cultural: references to shared knowledge.

CodeIn Kiss of the Vampire
HermeneuticSuspense surrounds the connoted relationship between the male and female vampires (emphasised by the “kiss” of the title) and the fate of their two victims. What are they to each other, and what happens next?
ProaireticThe scene is frozen mid-action: bats swoop, blood drips, victims are held. We expect an attack to follow.
SemanticThe bats carry their conventional association with vampirism and horror in general; blood and fangs reinforce the genre.
SymbolicHorror, darkness and fear are reinforced through signifiers such as the moon and the male victim’s “submissive sacrifice” gesture code.
CulturalA 1960s audience is assumed to know monster-movie poster conventions (composition, fonts, “the monster” and its usually female victims) and Hammer’s earlier hits.
In Kiss of the Vampire

Both vampires are positioned above the people they hold, who are on their knees with their heads thrown back, connoting submission. The male vampire stands behind the female and in the dark, yet he still keeps the audience’s focus.

3

Genre, conventions and intertextuality

Definition

Genre is a category of texts sharing codes and conventions. The monster movie genre centres on innocent people’s lives being threatened by a monster (supernatural, abnormally sized animals or other types of monster). It can also include horror, comedy, fantasy and science fiction elements. Intertextuality is when a text refers to, or can be compared with, other texts.

In Kiss of the Vampire
  • Typography: the capitalised, serif title has a “wooden” look, perhaps referencing the vampire’s coffin or the stake needed to kill him. Blood drips from the V’s “fang”.
  • Painted artwork: highly conventional for films of the period and echoing the poster for Christopher Lee’s Dracula.
  • “In Eastman Color”: anchors the colour image and connotes a modern telling of an older story.
  • Colour palette: gloomy grey, black and brown, with a red highlight that draws the eye to the bats, the vampire and the blood.
  • Star billing: the more highly paid male actors are listed first, in order of fame. Clifford Evans had starred in Hammer’s 1961 hit The Curse of the Werewolf.
  • Product context: it was intended to be the second sequel to 1958’s Dracula, though the script does not mention Stoker’s character. By 1963 Hammer also had success with The Mummy and Frankenstein films, and Universal had early success in the genre.

Genre iconography

Intertexts to compare: see the Hammer posters in “Going further”.

4

Stereotypes, countertypes and representation Hall

Definition

For Stuart Hall, representation is the production of meaning through signs. Media construct versions of reality. A stereotype reduces a group to a few simple, fixed characteristics; a countertype is a representation that challenges or contradicts a stereotype. Repeated representations feed a shared conceptual map of beliefs, values and expectations.

Reinforced stereotypesChallenged stereotypes (countertypes)
  • Clothing: both women wear long, silky dresses that emphasise their curves; the light colour suggests femininity and the delicate fabric the “gentle nature” of women.
  • Body language (left): on her knees, throat bare and head back, she connotes the submissive victim. The vampire holds her by one arm while protecting himself from bats, so he seems strong and dominant and she seems to be his property (or his source of sustenance).
  • Body language (right): this woman is in a position of power. Her facial expression is aggressive, and she is holding a man who is on his knees.
  • He is a victim being saved by a woman, an unusual gender dynamic for the time.
Context: the 1960s
  • The 1960s is often seen as the start of women’s sexual liberation, helped by the introduction of the contraceptive pill in 1960.
  • More women than ever entered paid work, and feminists campaigned for equal pay, an end to sexual harassment and greater equality. Equal pay legislation was passed in America in 1963.
  • Both older stereotypes of women as passive victims and more modern “male fears” of women challenging male dominance can be seen as encoded in the poster.
  • 1963 also saw early “Beatlemania” and the “swinging sixties”, the assassination of JFK, and the Soviet Union launching the first woman into space.
5

Identity Gauntlett

Definition

David Gauntlett argues that our identities are constructed through the media we consume and the representations on offer. People “pick and mix” from the role models and ideas that media provide.

In Kiss of the Vampire

The dominant female figure can act as a representation of women fighting the oppression of men. The poster can speak to many women of the period who were fighting for equality in the workplace and offer them a more powerful identity to engage with. The submissive victim on the left offers an older, more limited identity.

6

Spectacle and binary oppositions van ZoonenLévi-StraussA Level

Definition

Liesbet van Zoonen uses spectacle for the way media present women as objects to be looked at, often for an assumed male audience. Lévi-Strauss argued that texts create meaning through binary oppositions, pairs of opposites that we understand by contrast.

In Kiss of the Vampire: spectacle
  • Both women are young, conventionally attractive white women in alluring clothing, apparently inviting the attention of the men in the film and of the assumed male audience of a 1960s film, when attitudes were openly sexist.
  • The poster strays from convention because one woman is physically powerful and both male characters appear weak or cowardly: one is seemingly unconscious and kneeling, while the vampire recoils as if in shock. In horror of the time women were usually prey for a monster who was often coded as masculine.
In Kiss of the Vampire: binary oppositions
  • Vampires / victims: dominance against submission.
  • “Kiss” / monster: the romantic connotations of the title opposed to the stereotypical vampire.
  • Powerful woman / powerless woman: the right and left women.
  • Strong man / weak man: the male vampire, who both dominates and recoils, and the kneeling male victim.
Going further

The wider theory behind the toolkit

Hall: shared conceptual maps and how they shift

Hall argues that repeated representations feed shared understandings. Here, the body language of the woman on the left plus vampire iconography (bats, vampire clothing, teeth, castles, an eerie setting) feed an individual’s conceptual map. Repeated across many texts they form a shared conceptual map that tends to maintain beliefs and expectations about women and vampire films.

But challenging representations of gender can shift that map. The aggressive, dominant woman suggests the map might reshape to include women in positions of power and control.

Links: Gauntlett (do audiences take up the new identity?) · van Zoonen (media and social change) · Barthes (myth)

Reading positions: how might audiences have read the poster?
ReadingApplied to the poster
PreferredA thrilling monster film, with a familiar mix of horror and romance, aimed at a ticket-buying audience that knows the genre.
NegotiatedThe audience accepts the genre pleasures but notices the unusual power of the woman on the right.
OppositionalThe poster is read as sexist spectacle that objectifies women. Or the powerful woman is read as a positive sign of women’s liberation, against the intended meaning of a male-oriented horror image.

Links: Hall (encoding and decoding) · van Zoonen (assumed male audience)

van Zoonen: spectacle and social change A Level

Van Zoonen’s idea of spectacle helps explain how the women are styled and posed, and her wider argument is that media can contribute to social change by representing women in non-traditional roles.

Evaluation: the powerful woman might be a countertype and a sign of change. But you could also argue her power is contained within the genre: she is a vampire, a monster, so power for women is coded as threatening. The poster may reflect male fears about women’s liberation as much as celebrate it.

Links: Hall (stereotype and countertype) · Gauntlett (identity) · hooks (see below)

bell hooks and Gilroy: who is represented?

bell hooks’ intersectionality reminds us that gender interacts with race and class, and her work on patriarchal oppression asks whose power is being shown. Paul Gilroy’s postcolonial ideas ask who is treated as the norm and who as “other”.

  • Both women are young, conventionally attractive and white. The challenge to gender stereotypes does not extend to other identities.
  • Questions to explore: whose liberation does the 1960s context describe? Which women are missing from the poster? How is the monster positioned as an “other” in horror conventions?

Links: van Zoonen (women as spectacle) · Hall (stereotyping) · Lévi-Strauss (us / them oppositions)

Intertexts: how other Hammer posters represent women

Compare how women are positioned, sized and posed in these posters. Does Kiss of the Vampire look more conventional or more unusual by comparison?

Evaluation points for exam answers

  • Reinforce or challenge? A strong answer argues that the poster does both: it keeps older stereotypes (the victim) while showing a countertype (the dominant woman).
  • Reflect or construct? Does the poster simply reflect 1960s tensions, or help shape how audiences think about women’s power?
  • Limits of one text: a single poster is weak evidence that conceptual maps change. Support your argument with context and intertexts.
  • Contained challenge: the powerful woman is a monster, so is the challenge real or does the genre make female power frightening?
  • Judge by the period: avoid assuming that 1963 audiences read the poster as today’s audiences do.

Applying the ideas

Kiss of the Vampire: sign → denotation → connotation → underlying idea

SignDenotationConnotationUnderlying idea
Woman on the left, on her kneesHead thrown back, throat bare, held by one armSubmission, vulnerability, lack of powerThe woman as victim, reinforcing a stereotype (Hall). Women as spectacle (van Zoonen).
Woman on the right, holding a manAggressive expression; a kneeling man in her gripPower, dominance, threatA countertype reflecting 1960s challenges to male dominance (Gauntlett).
Kneeling manHead bowed, seemingly unconsciousWeakness, helplessnessReversal of the usual male rescuer role; “male fears” of women’s power.
Red blood and bats against grey and blackDripping blood, attacking bats, a gloomy paletteDanger, horror, and romance (“Kiss”)Genre conventions; semantic and symbolic codes (Barthes).
Title with “Kiss” and blood dripping from the VWooden-style capitals; blood dropsRomance against violence; stake and coffinAn enigma about the vampires’ relationship (hermeneutic code); binary of romance and monster (Lévi-Strauss).
“In Eastman Color”Yellow box with the textModern, technologically newA modern retelling of an older story; anchorage (Barthes).
Billing block with male stars firstCast names in order, then Hammer and UniversalFame, reliability, brand trustIndustry conventions of star billing; Hammer as a trusted horror brand.

Extra example 1: Dracula (1958) poster Same genre

SignDenotation / connotationUnderlying idea
Woman bent backwards in Dracula’s armsLimp, passive; connotes surrender and vulnerabilityThe woman as prey; the conventional stereotype that Kiss of the Vampire partly repeats (Hall).
“The terrifying lover who died – yet lived!”Tagline linking horror and romanceBinary of lover / monster; anchors the image (Barthes, Lévi-Strauss).
Compare: Dracula keeps the woman as passive prey; Kiss of the Vampire adds a second woman who dominates. What changed between 1958 and 1963?

Extra example 2: Tide (1950s print advert) Section A

SignDenotation / connotationUnderlying idea
Woman hugging the Tide box, hearts aboveSmiling housewife; connotes love and devotionReinforces the domestic housewife stereotype (Hall).
“Tide’s got what women want!”Confident headline speaking for all womenAnchors the image; presents a stereotype as natural (myth).
Compare: Tide reinforces one stereotype consistently for female consumers; Kiss of the Vampire mixes reinforced stereotypes and countertypes for a mainly male assumed audience. Why might the decade and the genre make the difference?

Extra example 3: Super. Human. (Channel 4, Tokyo 2020) Section A

SignDenotation / connotationUnderlying idea
“Super” shatters, leaving “Human”The word breaks like glass; connotes breaking a false imageChallenges the stereotype of disabled athletes as superheroes (Hall: countertype).
Compare: both texts challenge a stereotype, but one does so in a horror poster aimed at ticket buyers and the other in a public-service broadcaster’s advert. How does the purpose and audience shape the challenge?
Quick revision

Theorist grid

Roland Barthes

Media language

Semiotics. Denotation, connotation, myth, anchorage and the five narrative codes.

Poster: “Kiss” as enigma; red as danger and romance; bats as semantic code.

Claude Lévi-Strauss

Media language

Structuralism. Meaning is made through binary oppositions.

Poster: vampire / victim; romance / monster; powerful / powerless.

Stuart Hall

Representation · Audiences

Representation constructs meaning; stereotypes and shared conceptual maps. Preferred, negotiated and oppositional readings.

Poster: stereotype of the victim and countertype of the dominant woman.

David Gauntlett

Representation

Identity is built by picking and mixing from the representations media offer.

Poster: dominant woman as an identity for women seeking equality.

Liesbet van Zoonen

Representation

Feminist theory. Gender is constructed in media; women as spectacle; media can contribute to social change.

Poster: both women as spectacle, with a powerful woman and weak men as unconventional.

bell hooks

Representation

Intersectionality and patriarchal oppression: gender interlocks with race and class.

Poster: both women young, attractive and white; who is missing?

Paul Gilroy

Representation

Postcolonial theory. Ethnicity and “otherness”: who is treated as the norm and who as “other”.

Poster: the default woman is white; the monster as “other”.

David Hesmondhalgh

Industries

Cultural industries. Companies reduce risk by relying on proven formulas, stars, brands and sequels.

Link: Hammer’s franchises and sequels.

Livingstone & Lunt

Industries

Regulation, and audiences positioned as citizens or consumers.

Link: age restrictions and “Cert X” on horror posters.

Connections

Section A ↔ Section B

Kiss of the Vampire is only studied for Section A, so you will not be asked about it in Section B. But its techniques and ideas transfer to the Section B texts.

  • Hesmondhalgh (risk minimisation): the poster promotes a film intended as a sequel in a proven franchise, and Hammer repeated its monster formulas (Dracula, The Mummy, Frankenstein). Compare franchise logic in Black Panther and Assassin’s Creed.
  • Marketing: a poster is part of how a film is sold. The billing block, studio brand and star order are industry signals you can compare with Black Panther and I, Daniel Blake.
  • Livingstone & Lunt (regulation): the “Cert X” on the Hammer posters you compared in “Going further” shows film certification restricting who could see a film. Compare modern age ratings.
  • Representation across texts: use the stereotype / countertype toolkit to compare how women and other groups are represented in Black Panther, newspapers and the Tide advert.
